text.title: Accessibility Basics Worked Example
text.summary: One full end-to-end worked example demonstrating a typical report produced by this methodology, plus the most frequent accessibility failures in web code — form labels, image alt text, keyboard access, ARIA misuse — with before/after examples and antipatterns.

section.title: Example trace
section.p: A typical 5-minute quick-check on a small signup page produces 3 findings tagged with POUR + WCAG SC.

example.title: Quick-check on /signup
example.code: Scope: https://example.com/signup, WCAG 2.2 AA, owner @ruslan. Scanner findings (axe): - SC 1.4.3 [Perceivable, high]: Hero subtitle contrast 3.1:1. - SC 1.3.1 [Perceivable, medium]: Submit button placeholder-only label. Manual findings: - Tab pass: focus trapped inside cookie banner. Coverage statement: scanner catches ≈30%; manual + AT + user-testing required for full coverage. Verdict: partial.
example.note: Each finding carries SC number, POUR principle, severity, and source (scanner / manual).

section.title: Form labels
section.p: Every form input must have a visible, programmatically associated label. Placeholder text is not a label substitute: it disappears when typing and has insufficient contrast. Screen readers announce the associated label on focus; without it, blind users cannot determine the field's purpose. Low-contrast placeholders fail SC 1.4.3. (Same rule as placeholder-is-not-a-label in 01-core-rules.xml; the canonical rule governs.)

example.title: Placeholder as the only label
example.note: No label; placeholder disappears on input; screen reader announces only type.

example.title: Visible label with programmatic association
example.code: We'll never share your email.
example.note: Visible label, programmatic association, hint text linked via aria-describedby.

example.title: Decorative, informative, and complex images
example.note: Pattern follows alt-text-by-image-role in 01-core-rules.xml: the image's role in the page decides the alt strategy.
